title: Lower Egypt
capsule: During the window of c. 2200–2000 BCE—the First Intermediate Period following the collapse of the Old Kingdom—Lower Egypt and the Nile Delta fell under the Herakleopolitan kings of the Ninth and Tenth Dynasties, who ruled from Herakleopolis (Henen-nesut) near the entrance to the Faiyum. These rulers, many bearing the name Khety, claimed legitimate kingship over the whole land but in practice exercised only fragmentary authority over the Delta, contending with assertive local nomarchs and with a rival Theban line to the south. The instructional text known as the Teaching for King Merikare, set in this milieu, advises a Herakleopolitan heir on governance and on guarding the eastern Delta frontier against Asiatic incursions. The dynasty's hold ended when the Theban king Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II defeated the last Herakleopolitan ruler and reunified Egypt around 2055–2040 BCE, inaugurating the Middle Kingdom.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial extent is inferred from the Nile Delta geography; the precise boundaries and political structure of predynastic Lower Egypt are poorly attested, with royal names known only from the fragmentary Palermo Stone.
